content: Bicarbonate, also known as hydrogen carbonate according to IUPAC nomenclature, is an intermediate product formed during the deprotonation of carbonic acid (H₂CO₃). Structurally, the bicarbonate ion consists of a central carbon atom surrounded by three oxygen atoms arranged in a trigonal planar geometry, with one of the oxygen atoms bonded to a hydrogen atom. The bicarbonate ion carries a formal charge of -1 and acts as the conjugate base of carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) while also serving as the conjugate acid of the carbonate ion (CO₃²⁻). This dual role is demonstrated in the following equilibrium reactions: CO₃²⁻ + 2 H₂O ⇋ HCO₃⁻ + H₂O + OH⁻ ⇋ H₂CO₃ + 2 OH⁻ H₂CO₃ + 2 H₂O ⇋ HCO₃⁻ + H₃O⁺ + H₂O ⇋ CO₃²⁻ + 2 H₃O⁺ Bicarbonate salts are formed when positively charged ions bind to the negatively charged oxygen atoms of the bicarbonate ion, resulting in ionic compounds. Many bicarbonate salts, such as sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) and magnesium bicarbonate, are highly soluble in water under standard temperature and pressure conditions. These compounds contribute to the total dissolved solids (TDS) in water, a key parameter for evaluating water quality. Physiological Role Bicarbonate plays a critical role in the body's pH buffering system, which is essential for maintaining homeostasis. Approximately 86–90% of the carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the body is converted into carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), which can rapidly dissociate into bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). Acting as a central intermediate, carbonic acid, in conjunction with bicarbonate, water, hydrogen ions, and carbon dioxide, forms a dynamic buffering system. This system operates at a volatile equilibrium, enabling the body to resist sudden and drastic changes in pH in both acidic and basic directions. This buffering mechanism is particularly vital for protecting the tissues of the central nervous system (CNS). Deviations in pH outside the normal physiological range, whether toward acidosis or alkalosis, can have catastrophic consequences for CNS function and overall health. Other Uses The most commonly encountered bicarbonate salt is sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃), widely known as baking soda. When exposed to an acid, such as acetic acid (found in vinegar), bicarbonates release carbon dioxide gas. This reaction is utilized as a leavening agent in baking, where the release of carbon dioxide helps dough rise. Bicarbonate also plays a significant role in the carbon cycle. It is released from rocks during weathering processes caused by carbonic acid in rainwater, contributing to the global carbon cycle. In the digestive system, bicarbonate serves an important function by neutralizing stomach acid. After the highly acidic digestive juices have completed their role in breaking down food, bicarbonate raises the internal pH of the stomach, ensuring proper conditions for subsequent digestive processes.
